sections.title: How does the Car vs. Bike calculator work?
sections.html:
The Car vs. Bike calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance to workplace (one-way) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the congestion level and the engine type and prod. year); then you type in the biking speed, the fuel economy, the other car-related expenses and the extra life expectancy.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilometers per hour. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 35 options, such as petrol 2000 or older, petrol 2001 and petrol 2002. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Car vs. Bike calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Distance to workplace (one-way)=(5000 ÷ 521429) × extra life expectancy × biking speed ÷ (I commute × calculate the benefits over the next...)
Planted trees equivalent=(125 ÷ 2721552) × CO₂ emissions reduction ÷ calculate the benefits over the next...
Distance to workplace (one-way)=(1400000000 ÷ 1461) × (-other car-related expenses × calculate the benefits over the next... + money saved) ÷ (I commute × fuel economy × gas price × calculate the benefits over the next...)
Time saved=(1461 ÷ 70) × I commute × distance to workplace (one-way) × calculate the benefits over the next... × (18 × biking speed − 5 × average car speed) ÷ (biking speed × average car speed)
CO₂ emissions reduction=(1461 ÷ 14000) × CO₂ emissions × I commute × distance to workplace (one-way) × calculate the benefits over the next...
NOₓ emissions=(14000 ÷ 1461) × nOₓ emissions reduction ÷ (I commute × distance to workplace (one-way) × calculate the benefits over the next...)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Speed, opening in kilometers per hour
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Fuel economy, opening in liters per 100 kilometers
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years
  • Time, opening in days

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Car vs. Bike calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the biking speed, the fuel economy and the other car-related expenses — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Car vs. Bike calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance to workplace (one-way), derived from the biking speed, the fuel economy and the other car-related expenses. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Car vs. Bike calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the biking speed, the fuel economy, the other car-related expenses and the extra life expectancy, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance to workplace (one-way) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance to workplace (one-way) opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Average car speed = 0 km/h. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Car vs. Bike calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
